utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Just for your information, we'll be sitting today until 2.30, with two half-an-hour breaks. Good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we begin by having you state your name and your current position, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I am Major-General David Fraser, the commander of the 1st Canadian Division in Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Fraser, you have testified here at the Tribunal before, and that was in the case of Prosecutor versus Galic, in July of 2002, and in the case of the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic, in February of 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in 1997, in November of that year, you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review an amalgamated statement which represented excerpts from those previous testimonies and statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can we call up 65 ter 90196, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Fraser, do you recognise that, which bears your signature, as an electronic copy of the amalgamated statement which you indicated you had the opportunity to review?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does that statement accurately reflect your previous statements and testimony, or those portions of the previous statement and testimonies?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if you were examined in court today on the same subjects, would you provide the same information to the Court in response to those questions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would tender for admission 65 ter 90196, the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1762.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we would also be seeking the admission of the associated exhibits. I would note, for the Court's information, that with the exception of 65 ter 01302, a letter dated 9 October 1994, all of the documents that were indicated as previously admitted into evidence were. That document has been since admitted into evidence as P1644, and I think that updates the admission of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The only question from me is whether 11067 has been up-loaded. Otherwise, unless they are objected to, they will be admitted, and we'll give them an exhibit number in due course by the Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With the Court's permission, then, I would read a short summary of the statement -- the amalgamated statement and the witness's testimony. Major-General David Fraser was the military assistant to UNPROFOR's Sector Sarajevo commander from April 1994 to May 1995. He is a serving commander with the Canadian Armed Forces, with over 30 years of experience, experience which includes command of mortar platoons and military formations with snipers. As military assistant, General Fraser accompanied the sector commander in his daily tasks, including meeting with leaders of the warring factions at the corps level. General Fraser observed that both General Galic and General Milosevic enjoyed effective command and control over the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. For example, after protesting sniping incidents, Sarajevo would enjoy a noticeable decline in sniping for a period. General Fraser also concluded that the corps commanders were effectively subordinated to their higher military authorities and that policies, such as freedom of movement of UNPROFOR, were controlled at a higher level than the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. General Fraser observed that the objective of the Bosnian Serbs' siege of Sarajevo was to maintain pressure on the city rather than to take the city itself. Means used included controlling movement, modulating the amount of humanitarian aid allowed in, and employing sniping and shelling. The shelling employed by the Bosnian Serbs was indiscriminate; for example, UNPROFOR observed shelling in the city where there was no military target they could identify. Often, the Bosnian Serb forces disproportionately retaliated to Muslim provocations. In one instance, General Fraser recalled the Muslims firing on Lukavica, which provoked a "huge barrage" on the city in response. The Bosnian Serbs employed professional snipers who did not discriminate between military targets and civilians. In response to the sniping of civilians, barriers were placed throughout Sarajevo to protect civilians, and UNPROFOR established an anti-sniping task force. In these circumstances, General Fraser recalls that the civilians he met expressed to him the uncertainty and terror of never knowing what was going to happen next, and he observed that civilians he met were "visibly traumatised." Incidents of sniping and shelling were protested to both warring factions based on information obtained through crater analyses, by the Anti-Sniping Task Force, and other investigations. General Fraser recalls that toward the end of his tour, the Bosnian Serbs began to employ air-bombs in Sarajevo, a weapon he describes as a "make-shift apparatus with no guidance system." He did not observe such weapons on the Bosnian Government side. In General Fraser's opinion, these weapons had no military value. He recalls that the advent of the use of these weapons "sent shudders through all of us." Your Honour, that concludes the summary. And before I proceed, Mr. President, I would note that 65 ter 11067 is up-loaded and has been released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Fraser, let me first turn our attention to the issue of shelling, and I wanted to ask you a bit more about some of the shelling you observed and mentioned in your statement. Now, you referred in your statement, at page 52, to the targeting of civilian areas and, on page 53 of your statement, to shelling in which no distinction was made between military targets or civilians. Now, with respect to military targets, let me ask you this: First of all, however obvious this question may seem, were you aware that there were soldiers and military units in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you aware that there were headquarters of various units in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection, what was the major headquarters, the prime or corps -- highest-level headquarters of the Bosnian Serb forces in the Sarajevo area, and also of the Bosnian Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: There was the Bosnian Muslim 1st Corps headquarters in the city, the Serbian Romanija Corps headquarters just on the outskirts of the airport, and there was the defence headquarters down-town, for the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, would those corps headquarters -- the 1st Corps headquarters and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps headquarters, would those have represented the major or ultimate or most significant military targets in that area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: They would have represented the command and control for all the military forces in this region. They would have been the key -- keynotes in that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how frequently or how often those military targets were shelled?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Throughout my entire time that I was there, neither one, with the exception of one case, were those headquarters engaged, and the only time was late in my tour in 1995 when, in fact, the Muslims fired at the Lukavica Barracks, when we received a report from our own people there, which we found quite shocking, and it resulted in a very large barrage coming back from the Serbs against the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall the -- you alluded to it, but do you recall the nature of the shelling of Lukavica by the Bosnian forces, the type of weaponry and the amount, on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The Muslims fired at Lukavica with mortars. And in -- we protested the Muslim forces for doing that because of our concern with the reaction which followed through, which was both a heavy artillery barrage with heavy-calibre weapons back at the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say "back at the city," was the shelling by the Bosnian Serb forces, following the mortar shelling of Lukavica, directed at the Bosnian 1st Corps headquarters or was it directed elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The shelling did not come back at the Bosnian Corps headquarters. It seemed to be indiscriminate across the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how extensive was it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It was disproportional. There were -- where there were a few rounds fired at the Serbs, there were at least 20-plus rounds coming back, if not more, from my recollection. But it was a substantial reply back from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about some of the weapons systems used during or in the course of the shelling. First of all, you referred to mortars, and I know you commanded mortar platoons. For what purposes are mortars normally used? Are they directed at military structures, directed at military personnel? What's the primary use of mortars?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The principal use of mortars would be in support of infantry operations. They are most effective with dismounted people in the open, and they have limited value against any infrastructure or building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are they a precision-targeting system or an area weapons system?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: They are an area weapons system with a high trajectory, with quite a large beaten zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are they capable of pin-pointing particular targets, particularly in densely-populated areas?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: They are not a very good weapons system nor one that most commanders would use in a heavily urban, densely-populated area. They are better used out in the open.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, I noted that you -- in one of your responses, you indicated, "They are an area weapons system with a high trajectory, with quite a large beaten zone." Could you explain the term "beaten zone."

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Indirect fire weapons, like mortars or artillery, for the most part, do not have a guidance system on the warhead. It is a weapon that is fired using tables that, depending on the trajectory, it has a probability of landing in an area that can be calculated through tables which we'll use, weather/distance trajectory. Therefore, because we employ them as area weapons system, we use a box, a beaten zone where we think that the rounds will land and we don't use them as a precision-guided weapon, like a rifle or a tank. They are designed to provide area coverage, not pin-point coverage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's assume, for the purposes of this question, that a mortar round lands on a particular building within a densely-populated civilian area. Say it lands on, in fact, a military facility within that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is leading the witness to guess-work and speculation. Why should an examination-in-chief be conducted in such a manner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Tieger, you can reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not seeking any speculation, Your Honour. I'm about to ask the witness what the effect of a mortar round on a building is going to be. And there was no prospect, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not in relation to speculation, but there was some part of your question which may be said to be leading, to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll reformulate the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I was about to ask you: If a mortar round lands on a building or hits a building, what's the effect on that building and the people inside that building going to be? And I'd like you to particularly refer to the types of buildings in which any of the various units of the Bosnian Muslim Army might have been headquartered.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The buildings that we saw in and around Sarajevo were principally constructed of concrete, and any buildings that might have had Bosnian Muslim Army units inside them were inside these buildings. And the mortars that would be fired at these buildings would have little to no effect because of the construction of the building and the size of the mortars, which were either -- for the most part, around 82 millimetres; they were just too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What's the effect going to be on persons in the beaten zone, where the mortar might land; for example, civilians who are in the area and exposed to that fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Mortars fired at buildings would have little effect, but they would be effective for any unprotected people in the open.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you indicated in your statement that toward the latter part of your tour of duty in Sarajevo, Bosnian Serb forces began to employ air-bombs, which you described as a bomb that has -- I'm referring to page 63 of your statement now -- that has some sort of make-shift apparatus so that it can be used as a vehicle that can fly, but has no guidance system. And I think you said: "You just aim it, you launch it, and it will go wherever the ballistics capabilities and the aerodynamic capabilities of this improvised device are, and it lands based on if it runs out of fuel or, more likely, the aerodynamics of it are it just flops down." General, what's the military value of such a weapon?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In my opinion, there is no military value of this type of weapon inside an urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so what's the purpose, in your view, of launching such a weapon?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This type of weapon would be an indiscriminate use of a weapons system that would have more detrimental effects on non-combatant civilians and infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I'd like to direct your attention to a document. That would be 65 ter 10691. It's a document dated 7 April 1995, and it's a regular combat report of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command by General Milosevic. And, General, if I could turn your attention, please, to page 2 of the English and also page 2 of the B/C/S. And, in particular, if I could turn your attention to the passage in the middle of the page that states: "In Ilidza PBR, one 120-millimetre mine was fired and one 250-kilogram aerial bomb was launched at the center of Hrasnica. According to the interception centre, the Muslims claimed that the 'Luna' rocket had landed." General, is this a reference to one of the aerial bombs that you mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what kind of area was Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Hrasnica was essentially a civilian area just at the foot of the Igman Mount.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could quickly direct your attention also to a passage at the top of page 3 of the English, and I believe that's still page 2 of the B/C/S, and that refers to an incident involving fire between the Bosnian Serb forces and UNPROFOR. We may have occasion to refer to that later, but I wondered if you remembered that incident.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell us quickly what happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The Igman Mount route was being used by civilians to go in and out of the town. The Serbs had been engaging the route. We had protested against the Serbs from engaging that route. It resulted in us placing UN soldiers on the route to protect it. And notwithstanding that, the Serbs continued to fire not just at the route, but, in fact, firing at us. And, in fact, it got to the point where they had literally out-gunned us with -- our weapons systems could not effectively reply to the systems that they were firing at us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I was asking principally about the issue of air-bombs, and --

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, you answered my question. I just want to return us to what I had been focusing on previously. And in that connection, if I could ask you to direct your attention to another document, and that is P1201. That's a document of April 6th, and that will be coming up on screen shortly, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has the previous document been admitted, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It has not, and I would move it into admission at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1782, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Fraser, P1201 is an order from the Sarajevo Romanija Command, from General Milosevic. It states that: "The Ilidza Brigade will immediately prepare a launcher with an aerial bomb and transport the bomb for launching. "The most profitable target must be selected in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Colony, where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted. "Inform me personally of readiness for implementation of this task." First of all, General, although -- well, let me ask you: Is there, in your view, a relationship between this order of April 6th and the combat report of April 7th that you saw just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: There seems to be a correlation between the two, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in your experience, what is this order tasking the Ilidza Brigade to do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: From my reading of the order, I would say that they are asking the Serb forces to fire at a, essentially, civilian population and not at the route or the UN forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is that an order of the type that you have -- that would be issued by you or that you would permit to be issued by a subordinate?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: From my read of this order, I would see it as a manifestly unlawful order. And as a recipient of this order, I would actually not abide by it because of the not addressing a target that was legitimate and principally a target that was civilian and that would inflict casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, let's assume for the moment -- or let me ask you this: What if there was a unit of the Bosnian Muslim Army in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Colony? Would that change the illegal nature of launching an air bomb, as specified in this order?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The air-bomb would be a completely inappropriate weapon to fire at a military target in an area that is as densely populated as this town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you indicated what you learned about the command and control of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps with respect to shelling and sniping and other issues during the course of your tour of duty. In your assessment, what level of command would have been in a position to authorise or ratify the use of air-bombs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: My assessment was that the corps commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had direct control over the use of shelling and sniping inside and around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me ask you to look at another document. That's P1294, and that's a document of 12 June 1994. General, this is an order forwarded to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on 12 June 1994. It refers to the Ilijas Infantry Brigade's letter directly to the Main Staff, requesting that aerial bombs be issued by the Vogosca Pretis, and then provides, in the second paragraph, that: "The VRS Main Staff decides on the use of aerial bombs and possibly a corps, if the VRS Main Staff approves so, and not a brigade according to its own plan." General, is this document consistent with your observations during the course of your tour of duty, your communications with Bosnian Serb military leaders, and the situation on the ground as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This document confirms our assessment at the time that the corps was in control of all forces on the ground and they were operating under the direction of their higher headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I'd like to ask you a few questions about the sniping of civilians, to which you've referred in your statement. And at page 24 of your statement, General, you stated that the sniping on civilians was a matter of concern throughout your tour of duty, and further indicated that sniping of civilians took place by both sides, but mostly by the Serb side. And that would be found at page 24. Is that roughly accurate, General?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to ask you how you were able to determine which side was responsible -- on a given occasion or over the course of your tour of duty, which side was responsible for sniping incidents? Were there specific investigations? Did you have groups dedicated to the process? Through what sources did you determine responsibility for the sniping of civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The UN was tasked to ensure that we did not get involved between the confrontations between the two warring parties. Therefore, we took great care to determine whether or not that any sniping incident was between two warring factions. If so, we would stay out of it. But when it came to non-combatant civilians, we would engage with a protest, and we ensured that the protest was lodged to the right faction. And because of the urban terrain, we took particular care to determine which side fired the shot against a non-combatant. What we did was, for any incident, we would convene an investigation, either at the battalion or at the sector level, to determine whether or not the incident was fired at a civilian, which side fired the shot, and then we would protest to the applicable side. We had battalions on the ground responsible for looking at all these incidents. In addition, along the route commonly referred to as Sniper Alley, we had established an anti-sniping force which was designed to observe potential sniping positions, engage in those -- at those positions for snipers who were firing at civilians. And in addition to that, we had, as part of that task force, put into place passive barriers to protest civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, with respect to the Anti-Sniping Task Force, let me ask you first: What prompted the establishment of a special task force developed to -- dedicated to anti-sniping?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The amount of incidents in the city, in the area of Sniper Alley, against civilians necessitated that we create this task force, with specialised troops with reconnaissance/surveillance capabilities, to determine potential sniper positions. We had photographed and drawn out all the potential areas, in addition to having shooters to reply to these snipers, all designed to protect the citizens of Sarajevo. And certain areas, as I say, which were particularly open to snipers were enhanced with passive protection, but this was in response to the sniping being conducted in the city against civilians on trams and walking through the open areas of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did the Anti-Sniping Task Force become pretty familiar with where the snipers were positioned and -- where the snipers were and where they were firing from?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, the task force was very familiar with the sniper positions. On at least one occasion, I visited one of these positions with my French boss. And both warring factions knew where the Sniper Task Force was deployed because we were out in the open, and, in fact, we actually had UN soldiers shot and killed by snipers along this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you mentioned investigations, you mentioned the work of and observations of the Anti-Sniping Task Force, and you also mentioned discussions with Bosnian Serb military leaders. As far as the latter is concerned, I'll be asking you some questions about that in a moment, but let me ask you a couple of questions about the investigations and the Anti-Sniping Task Force. First, I wanted to ask you: With respect to your level of certainty regarding responsibility of one side or the other for individual sniping incidents -- and I'm going to ask you first about individual incidents, and I'm going to ask you about the totality of the sniping activities that were taking place. But, first, with respect to any individual incident, what was the level of certainty regarding responsibility, based on investigations or the input from the Anti-Sniping Task Force?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The Anti-Sniping Task Force were very good in determining the point of origin for specific incidents. And where they were able to, they would reply in kind back to the sniper. In the event that they could not, notwithstanding they might have replied, that information would have been sent up to the battalion and to the sector level, where in all cases we would have protested for each individual incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And based on all the information that was available to you from the Anti-Sniping Task Force, from specific investigations, from your discussions with Bosnian Serb military leaders, what was the level of certainty that Bosnian Serb forces were or were not engaged in ongoing sniping attacks against civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We were certain that the Bosnian Serbian forces were engaging against civilians. We had countless engagements with the corps commander to discuss sniping, and implored them to stop the sniping against civilians. And these discussions at the corps level, for the most part, would have some positive effect for a while, but it was only a temporary effect, and there was a constant cycle of situations getting worse, then getting a little bit better, and then getting worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with respect to that temporary positive effect, what, if anything, did that indicate to you about the command and control of the corps commander and of the Bosnian Serb military leadership of the sniping against civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It was our assessment that sniping was an activity that was controlled and regulated at the corps level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, about some of the other factors relating to command and control over sniping activities, particularly those against civilians that you referred to in your statement. And first let me ask you about the nature of snipers. I think you indicated, at page 31, that sniping is very specialised, involving a highly-skilled shooter who can move in and out of places without being seen and fire at targets of high value. Can you explain the relationship between the nature of a sniper, and a sniper's particular or unique expertise and value, and command and control?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Snipers are a very specialised skill that is taught to very few individuals, the best individuals. You have a combination of shooting and tactical skills to move on the battle-field without being seen. Because there are so few of them, they are traditionally maintained at the highest level for targets that are of particular importance to the commander on the field, and they are not to be wasted because of -- on any given target. They are designed to do something to inflict -- taking off and decapitating, metaphorically speaking, the command and control by taking out a commander or by instilling a disruptive effect on the enemy. But they are a very specialised skill that is judiciously used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you referred to a very specialised skill. Is that -- and how did you assess the skill level of the Bosnian Serb snipers in Sarajevo during the course of your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We had snipers within the UN that were designed to find other snipers across -- on the Serbian side. They assessed that they were dealing with a very professional force, because amateurs are killed very quickly, easily found, easily dealt with, and the people that we were looking for and were engaging in sniping against civilians were hard to find. They fired through buildings, which is a demonstration of a level of capability that not just an average shooter can do, and our snipers just had a really hard time to find these people. So, I mean, there was an assessment that these people were professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I want to ask you to look at three documents, all bearing on the same subject. So before I solicit any comment in response, I'll just give you an opportunity to quickly look those over. The first is 65 ter 15725, and that's a report of the 1st Ilijas Infantry Brigade to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command, dated 13 January 1995, pursuant to a training order with proposals. And if I could ask you to direct your attention to page -- first, page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S, and that's in the middle of the page. There's a reference to: "For instructors, those doing the training and physical training of snipers, who are going to attend a court," which I presume is "course," "by the end of January this year, we recommend the following people from our brigade:" And then if I could ask you quickly to direct your attention to page 3, also in the middle of the page, in English: "We recommend the following improvements and changes to the curriculum: "Sniper course: Number of classes for topic 3 to be increased to 15 from 13; the number of practices, 6." And next I would ask you to turn your attention to document 65 ter 15507. And I'll be asking the General to look quickly at page 4 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S. This is a report from the Command of the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command, and it's a report pursuant to a strictly-confidential order of January 5th. And as I indicated, I wanted to ask you to turn your attention to a portion on page 4, stating that: "We would recommend the following for training as snipers:" And then listing the names and indicating: "We recommend Lukavica as the location for training." And, finally, one last document in that connection, General, and that is P1613. This is an order from General Milosevic, from the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, dated 19 January 1995, regarding the detachment and transfer of sniper instructors to conduct training in the Jahorina Barracks, pursuant to the instruction and training of the VRS Main Staff. And if you just look at that quickly, General, you'll see the order specifies the date and time of transfer of sniper instructors to the sector of the Jahorina Barracks, and other information regarding that training, and specifies that the order must be carried out in full and: "... I shall hold the brigade commanders personally responsible." General Fraser, having looked at those orders, can you tell us whether -- those orders and reports, can you tell us whether those are consistent or inconsistent with your assessment of the capabilities and professionalism of the snipers engaged in Sarajevo on the Bosnian Serb side during the course of your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The orders and reports are indicative of the Serbs -- the importance they played on to training, and within the training, the importance within that of snipers is evident by the explanation in each one by name, of what snipers have a predominant mention in these training reports, and the last report confirms, in fact, our initial assessment when I was there, that this was a corps asset, personally controlled by the corps commander with this corps order that orders snipers and fuel and the transfers and holding brigade commanders personally responsible. You can't get much more specific than this that this is a corps commander's priority and his asset that he is controlling personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, in your amalgamated statement, you also indicated other factors that related to the command and control by the Bosnian Serb military leadership over snipers. One of them is found on page 25, where you state: "It is my opinion that these snipers were acting on orders from a higher organisation than the areas, because the three areas that I described, Sedrenik, Sniper Alley, and the airport, crossed across a number of different Serbian brigades." Can you tell the Court about the significance of the fact that sniping was taking place in various areas where various lower-level units were deployed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The sniping activity in the city seemed to have a pattern throughout the city which, when you looked at the division of brigades, it appeared to us at the time that there was somebody thinking and enacting a plan that was controlling the activity over the city and not just three independent brigades doing their thing. The fact that snipers are highly-specialised individuals, the pattern of activities, we just had the assessment that this was being co-ordinated at a higher level. The documents I've just read actually confirm our assessment at the time that this was actually a corps-driven asset and plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you referred earlier to meetings that you and other UN military officials had with Bosnian Serb military leaders to protest the sniping against civilians, and indicated that there would be at least a temporary decrease in sniping activity thereafter. At page -- I want to ask you about one other aspect of those meetings. I think at page 22 of your statement, you indicated the following: "I can characterise meetings with him starting off by being lectured, a denial of what it was we were trying to discuss. However, there was some acknowledgment about sniping around the city." And a general consensus that it would be nice if they had an anti-sniping agreement. And that was with respect to meetings with General Galic. Let me ask you to turn your attention, in that connection, to another document, document 65 ter 19248. And, Your Honour, before I move on to that document, if I may move into admission the two of the training-related documents referred to earlier. That's 65 ter 15725 and 65 ter 15507.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P1783 and P1784 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, 65 ter 19248, now on the screen, is a report on a meeting of June 24th, 1994. It's a report by General Galic of that meeting. And if I can direct your attention to the passage that begins toward the bottom portion of the page, after "Discussions and Conclusions," it states: "General Soubirou spoke about human aspect of the agreement on the cessation of the use of sniper arms. General Galic agreed that the use of snipers is inhuman, adding he opposed partial agreements, but stressed that a general agreement was possible." Then it goes on in the first person: "I accepted the explanation, but I underscored that the agreement signed on February 9th, 1994, included this problem as well. I especially stressed that the hitherto agreement has not been respected by the Muslim side, and that UNPROFOR has not done anything to make them respect the agreement." First of all, General, this is -- in this meeting between General Galic and General Soubirou, do you recall, at this point, whether you were present at that meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I believe I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does the -- well, first of all, is the account provided for in this report generally consistent with your recollection of how these meetings would -- how this particular meeting took place, and, more generally, how these meetings would proceed with respect to protests by the -- and expressions of concern by UNPROFOR and reactions by the Bosnian Serb military leadership?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This is typical for how meetings were conducted by the Serb corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the subject of the discussion sniping on civilians by both the Bosnian Serb forces and the Bosnian Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We did talk about the subject of sniping against civilians with both sides. We implored both sides to stop this activity because it was inhumane and it was not in accordance with any rules of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did General Galic deny that the Bosnian Serbs were engaged in sniping on civilians or did he protest that the Bosnian Muslims were also engaged in sniping on civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Traditionally, he would lecture and deny it at the beginning, and then over the course of the conversation would acknowledge that some of this was happening. He would blame the other side for this action. But normally after these meetings, there would be a slight amelioration in the situation. So from our inference, he would take note, and somewhere people would listen to him to improve the situation against civilians. But it was a temporary effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, in your amalgamated statement, you spoke about the Bosnian Serb effort to maintain control over the city through, among other things, restrictions on the amount of humanitarian aid. I believe that's found at page 5 of your statement, including keeping pressure on the city by controlling humanitarian aid. Was that a problem throughout the course of your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It was, indeed. They were very good at determining how much aid we had coming into the city, how much aid we had stockpiled in the city, and they regularly controlled that by either slowing down or stopping convoys. And at one stage, I do recall we ate -- we had no fresh food for 20 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to tender that report?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1785, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I asked you about command and control over other aspects of what was happening in Sarajevo or what was being done by Bosnian Serb forces in Sarajevo. Let me ask you, then, about the command and control over restrictions on humanitarian aid. And in that connection, if I could ask you to turn to 65 ter 07651. General, this is a report of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, dated 14 April 1994, to the president of Republika Srpska, the Commands of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and to other corps, as well as to the Main Staff of the Yugoslav Army. And if I could direct your attention to three -- two portions toward the latter part of the report, found at the bottom of page 3 in English, first, and page 3 of the B/C/S, which states as follows: "Situation in the territory: "During the day, there were no movements of teams and convoys of UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations across the territory of Republika Srpska. The decision made by the Supreme Command on restriction of movement is being implemented." And, similarly, if I could ask you to turn to the very end of the document, which states: "To continue with the consistent implementation of the decision of the Supreme Command on the suspension of relations with UN Forces Command and the restriction of movement for the teams and convoys of UNPROFOR and the humanitarian organisations." And, General, is this document consistent or inconsistent with your assessment of who controlled restrictions on humanitarian assistance during the course of your tour of duty in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This document is consistent with our assessment that humanitarian aid and our freedom of movement was being controlled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I want to ask you about two more documents related to -- Your Honour, before you have to ask me that, I would move this into admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1786, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to two more documents related to pressure on -- maintaining pressure on the city, as you mentioned at page 5, through pressure on humanitarian organisations and UNPROFOR. The first document is 65 ter 1331 [sic]. I'm sorry, that document should be 11331. General, we had an opportunity earlier to look at the event that happened on April 7th, 1995. This document is an order from General Milosevic of 26 November 1994 to the commander of the Ilijas Infantry Brigade, that states: "Following the oral order of the VRS Main Staff commander, immediately repeat the task according to my order Strictly Confidential ... from November 24th, 1994: "Pay attention to the consumption of ammunition. "I am to be personally informed about the completion of the task. "You are to fire at the center of deployed UNPROFOR forces." General, is this document consistent or inconsistent with your assessment, during the course of your tour of duty, of pressures placed on UN forces, including attacks on UN forces and the level of responsibility and command and control for those efforts?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This document is consistent with our assessments during the time I was there. It is also consistent with the attacks on our own UN forces, and it confirms that this was a direct contravention of the rules, of the corps commander directing his troops to fire upon the UN, and we were not at war or in conflict with the Serbian forces. Quite frankly, it disgusts me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One more document, General, and that is 65 ter 19250. General, this is an order from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, dated 13 April 1994, regarding treatment of the members of international organisations in the territory of Republika Srpska. And it's an order from General Mladic sent out to various command headquarters, and it states, in part: "UN Military Observers and the members of the UNPROFOR are to be accommodated in appropriate premises outside of the facilities where they had been stationed to date; that is, in the military facilities which are a potential target of the NATO Air Force, as per your choice." And then it goes on to specify that the -- that these UN Military Observers and members of UNPROFOR are to be forbidden phone and communication contact and prevented from contact with others, and to remain in isolation. Again, General, is this order from General Mladic consistent or inconsistent with your assessment at the time, based on your experiences on the ground, your military experience, your contacts with Bosnian Serb military leaders, and all the other factors available to you, about command and control over actions directed against UN forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This document is consistent with our experiences with the Serbian forces on the ground. It is evident of a very effective command-and-control system by General Mladic to his forces, who executed these conditions, I would say, and treated UN soldiers as prisoners of war even though we were not combatants in this faction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would move into evidence this document and the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, both of them will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 11331 will be Exhibit P1787, and 65 ter 09250 will be Exhibit P1788.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, General, I wanted to turn your attention to one other portion of your amalgamated statement and just clarify that completely. You stated at page 73 of your statement that you spent a lot of time -- you and other UN officials spent a lot of time moving around the city and talking to people, including local residents who worked for the UN. And during the course of that, you would ask them what life was like, and you said: "In all cases, they expressed the uncertainty and terror of never knowing what was going to happen next." And you could see that they were "visibly traumatised." This question was not explicitly asked, although given the context in which you're discussing it, so I just wanted there not to be any ambiguity about that. In respect of what caused this terror, what was it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This terror was the result of a number of different factors. The city was at -- sieged. Their humanitarian aid was being controlled by the Serbs. They were being shelled, they were being sniped at, and residents of the city never quite knew what was going to happen to them when they walked outside the door. And, therefore, every time they walked outside the door, they were taking their lives into their own hands. And as some of them said to me, and I will never forget it, in the 1940s, under the German regime, life was a lot better than it was during the Bosnian civil war, which is not a good thing to say. But in comparison, it just puts into context for me that it was absolutely the worst conditions for anybody to live in was in Sarajevo during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Shall we have a break before you start your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take the break for half an hour, and we'll resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If I may be allowed to reiterate once again that the time allocated to me for this important witness will not be sufficient, particularly since Mr. Tieger dealt with this witness in a very ambitious way, which provided us with a huge number of general statements. And with kind assistance of General Fraser, we will need to clarify those in order to make them objective and reliable. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General Fraser.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to thank you for your kindness and your communication, via videolink, with the Defence team, and I believe that we agreed on certain things that we are going to confirm and repeat here today. Would you agree with me that the Trial Chamber should disregard those portions of your statement that pertain to the periods when you were not stationed there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's up to me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you would agree that there are portions relating, for example, to Gorazde during the period while you were not there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'd like to advise you to move on to your next topic. It's not for the witness, as he indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that the Serbs did not seek assistance from the United Nations, while, on the other hand, the Muslims protested and asked for assistance. Can you please tell us: What kind of sources did you use as sources of information while stationed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you are seeking a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you indicate the reference you are citing from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to one portion of the statement. Now I have to find this particular part in the general's statement, and it will take a little time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall saying something like that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't recall. You'll have to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By my mistake, I read your statement of 1997, which I thought it was -- which was an amalgamated statement. On page 11 of that statement, there's a similar passage which goes to the effect that: "In fact, the Serbs never asked for our help. They had a fatalistic attitude and used as being the underdogs as part of their campaigns." Do you remember that kind of a passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do recall something like that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were you referring to that, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Thank you. But I wanted to ask the general to tell us and name the sources of his information, since the Serbs were not whining a lot, were not asking for assistance, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: Which particular sources of information did you use during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We would speak to the Serbian corps commander, and that's where my experience was limited with the engagements between my commander and the Serbian corps commander. We would engage on the Muslim side equally with the Muslim corps commander. In addition, my commander would engage with the leadership of the Muslim government and, on the odd occasion, would accompany General Rose to engage other Serbian leadership. So the source of our information was from Muslim or Serbian leaders, in addition to our own reports from our units from throughout Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you mean, by that that you used government reports or government agency reports produced by the government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I don't recall ever using government reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During our conversation, and also in your statements, you said that you had certain reservations concerning reports by military observers who were embedded with you but were unreliable and sent their reports first to Zagreb and then to you. This is what you said in your statement given on page 0055-5094, given between the 15th and 18th November 1997. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I do agree that I made comments about the utility of UNMOs. They were dependent -- their reliability was dependent on which nation they came from. And their reporting chain did go back to Zagreb, which made getting timely information from them difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say that the nationality of an UNMO and certain battalions did have a certain impact on reliability?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this page of the statement, number 0055-5094, 65 ter 11709 [as interpreted]. 11079.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you'd like to refer to this document later on, it may be a good idea to give a hard copy to the general in advance, if that can be arranged. I don't think this is -- I thought Mr. Karadzic referred to his earlier statement of 1997. Could you check the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 11079, that's the statement, and we need page 14, the ERN number is 0055-5094. This is not the document that I'm looking for. If we can kindly ask the Prosecution to provide the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I checked the filing from the Prosecution, and the 65 ter number is noted as 11079. Yes, it's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm that this is your statement from 1997? And then we need page 14. Can you please focus on the paragraph entitled "UN Military Observers." If you agree, sir, it says here that all of them, more or less, with the exception of certain individuals that you described as positive examples, the rest of them were rather unreliable and their reports were useless; in other words, that UNPROFOR commanders had to resort to using their own sources; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: What I said was that they were inconsistent, unreliable. The reporting chain was up to Zagreb. It goes back to what I said earlier, that for timely information we did rely on our own resources. And as part of a normal military chain, we would use multiple sources to try to corroborate information on the ground. And I just want to clarify. You said "battalions" earlier in your question. I'm just limiting my comment to UNMOs, United Nations Military Observers, as stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll later deal with the difference between various battalions. [In English] "They were inconsistent, unreliable and in fact they reported first to Zagreb, which wasn't of such use to us." [Interpretation] You can confirm this sentence that I have just read out to you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Wasn't of such use to us, yes, but wasn't completely dismissed. But they were unreliable, inconsistent, and we relied on other sources to put together the missing pieces or to corroborate what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see the previous page, which will hopefully shed some light on the structure and organisation of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, ERN 5083. The previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 93, then, page 13.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sorry, 83. 0055-5083. That's page 3 of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct. If Mr. Karadzic does not need the B/C/S page, we can collapse that part so that the general can see the more zoomed-in page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be useful to the interpreters, but anyway:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that here you established the existence of certain differences on the basis of nationality? For example, when you mentioned General Soubirou and Gobillard, these ADCs who were autonomous, to a certain extent, it says: [In English] "... the French sitreps and intelligence reports which Soubirou did not want any non-French person to read."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we'll need to scroll down to find the reference that was just made. Sorry, and if it's helpful, we have a hard-copy version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could that be handed over to the general. I take it there's no objection from the Defence. Yes, that's page 3, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm this, this part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The French did write reports that went back up their own national chain, and they kept those pretty much to themselves. I was not privy to everything that they wrote, and my duties were principally for the UN portion. And what they wrote from a French point of view was for French eyes only. But the fact that I was the military assistant did not prevent me from doing my jobs -- doing my job as a Canadian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that it would have been helpful if you could impart on us what was it that they wrote in their reports, although you didn't have access to those reports?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: As I said in my last sentence in the fourth paragraph, I had a look at them a couple of times, but there was nothing particularly striking in them. So it was essentially mainly reporting back information that was going back up UN channels. And under coalition operations, it is typical for nations to report back, up their own channels, what was going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the same practice pursued by other national contingents?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that we gave approval for the presence of the UN, but we did not give our approval for the presence of any national forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The fact that I was there under the UN auspices meant you were inviting Canada to participate as part of the UN membership, so I would say you approved both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that the Serbian side had its specific reasons to be suspicious of individual national contingents with regard to their impartiality, and that in that respect we preferred to rely on the UN rather than on individual national contingents, particularly those from NATO?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: When I was the -- I do not agree with you on that statement, because everybody who was wearing the blue beret was there under the UN auspices, we were there under a UN mandate, and notwithstanding that certain countries might have belonged to NATO, we were not there as NATO partners there, we were there as UN forces, and my commander took particular care to make sure that all the troops under his command acted in an impartial way to all of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, in your statement you say that to you it was more important who the commander was, whereas other officers in HQ were just a sort of window dressing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Can you indicate where I said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm if you said that, and then we'll find it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I would have to read my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's on the next page. Can we please have the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, I do say that: "The UN officers in the headquarters were essentially 'window dressing.'" That said, the French did the majority of the work, the meaningful work, and it was among -- it was a matter of efficiency that, to get things done, you leaned on those people within the headquarters that could get the work done, because we were talking about protecting and executing the UN mandate. It's in that context that I said that, I made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you said that, for example, General Soubirou received instructions from Generals Rose or Smith, but that basically he operated on the basis of consultations with his home country, which is France?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: General Rose and General Smith were General Soubirou's immediate superiors, and he would take orders from them. But in all coalition operations, we all come from various nations, and we take instructions and consultations from our respective nations. It's a function of coalition operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During our videolink conference, you confirmed that you were aware of the fact that the UN shared its information with NATO and that it was mainly done between General Rose and Admiral Leighton Smith; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I said I listened to several conversations on the phone between Rose and Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also confirmed your belief that UN sitreps and other sources of information had also been passed on to NATO.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I don't recall that I confirmed that the UN sitreps were passed on to NATO. I do confirm that Rose tried to explain the situation to NATO, and in many cases to explain the UN position on the ground, given the circumstances that the UN was facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have agreed -- or, rather, you have confirmed that General Rose brought in JCOs into Bosnia because he wanted to have independent and reliable sources of information. Those were, in fact, British soldiers that he could trust, and they were deployed in Gorazde, among other places, as members of the SAS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: General Rose did bring in the JCOs as another source of information. What they did in Gorazde, you would have to ask him. And they came from the British Army, and some of the soldiers were SAS, but not just exclusive to SAS, from my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In our conversation, you confirmed that you had knowledge -- or, rather, the UN had knowledge about the existence of the black market and the involvement on UN personnel in such transactions, and that there were even some investigations carried out about that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The UN were conducting investigations of allegations of black-marketeering by the UN, and this was taken very seriously and investigated by a task force that came out of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were even criminal vehicles that were blown up illegally, and those were vehicles [as interpreted] by those who were trying to prevent this. A French officer who was trying to prevent this was blown up; isn't that right? Let me rephrase this question. Is it correct that a vehicle of the commander of a French platoon, who was trying to prevent this black-marketeering, was blown up, and that this had to do with his activities aimed at countering the black-market activities?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: There was a French military police platoon commander who had his vehicle booby-trapped with a bomb. He was in the process of investigation -- investigating black-marketeering, and he did come to us and we put him and the proper police authorities on to the allegations of black-marketeering that he was looking into.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At our meeting, you claimed that the booby-trapping of this vehicle could have to do possibly with his activities against black-marketeering; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was also UN personnel that was involved in prostitution rings in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I've heard of those allegations, and any -- any allegations that we would have heard about, we would have brought the proper investigative authorities in to address those allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, during our conversation, that the UN CivPol carried out a major investigation into the smuggling activities involving ammunition, weapons, vehicles, fuel, people, identity cards, and alcohol; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: There was -- this was part of the UN task force on black-marketeering, and the sector conducted at least one major investigation on allegations of black-marketeering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this had to do with the smuggling of the articles that I just referred to and that you also referred to during our conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also agreed that because of this, Serbs did have reason to be cautious in approving the entry of convoys into Sarajevo, in light of this black-marketeering; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I did not agree to that. I would say that, in fact, black-marketeering was an issue that all warring factions had to deal with. And the UN took it very seriously and dealt with it, and we raised those issues with the appropriate side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you would agree, would you not, that the Serbs had reasons for increased caution and control of everything that was coming into Sarajevo, in light of this information?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I would not agree that the Serbs had to have increased control. I would say that the Serbs, in co-operation with the UN, should have looked at black-marketeering and to respect the UN mandate for freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During our conversation, I asked you to be more precise about freedom of movement. In your opinion, freedom of movement, especially for humanitarian convoys, would that imply the absence of control?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No, there has to be an element of control, but not to the point of restricting humanitarian convoys from reaching their destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the force that issues permission for the passage of humanitarian convoys, does that force have any right to pose certain conditions on the passage; for example, some technical conditions, things like that? Technical conditions.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Control would include technical conditions. But for the inference you say, the force that issues permission for the passage of humanitarian convoys, we weren't asking for permission, we were informing the Serbs that humanitarian supplies were coming into the city for humanitarian purposes, and just proper control measures should be taken to make sure that they got there, not to restrict them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now we are going to come to a certain misunderstanding, in the legal sense. Do you know, General, sir, that for the first time in the history of warfare, in the Serbian-Bulgarian War the Serbian military ceased their activities in order to allow humanitarian assistance for the Bulgarians to pass, and this then actually assisted the founder of the Red Cross to set this as a norm? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What relevance does it have, Mr. Karadzic? Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, there are so many bad things heard about Serbs, it's not a bad thing to hear something good. It was the Serbs who established this rule of allowing passage to humanitarian aid in the 19th century, and the Red Cross founder took that as the grounds for that particular norm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in any case, General, can we now look at 1D2612 so that we can clarify what are the rights of the parties. 1D2612. This is the 4th Convention that relates to the protection of civilian persons in time of war. Can we now look at page 23, please. I'm sorry, page 9, Article 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just as a housekeeping matter - I'm not objecting to the use of this document - I understand the documents may surface during the course of cross-examination that were not notified. It's a little unusual. The first one is in that category. But, in any event, if Dr. Karadzic could just advise us if he's using a document that has not been notified to the Prosecution so that we can -- it's not that -- so we don't go through the searching process to try to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Geneva Convention is not the sort document that is usually admitted during the course of examination, but your submission must have been noted by the Defence. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will do our best, of course. The need for this arises from our differing understanding of the rights of parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to Article 23, if you agree -- could you please look at it and see what the rights of the parties are. And then there is the place which says: "The power which allows the passage of the consignments indicated in the first paragraph of this article ..." [In English] "... may take such permission conditional on the distribution to the persons benefitted, thereby being made under the local supervision of the protecting powers. "Such consignments shall be forwarded as rapidly as possible, and the power which permits this free passage shall have the right to prescribe the technical arrangements under which such passage is allowed." [Interpretation] How was it possible for the Serbian side, General, to stop being one of the parties, and is no longer being asked for permission but is only being informed of matters?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: All I can say is that I've read now this, and it states very clearly in the first paragraph. And I guess my going -- question back would be: Understanding what this says, why is it that I went 20 days without having fresh food? Because in accordance with this, it should have been -- the food materials should have been provided as quickly as possible. I will not object, you know, for the -- what it states in here, for power which allows the passage, that's the third-last paragraph, I get that, but the intent of the first paragraph is very clear, is to deliver the humanitarian aid and the materials as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree. But do you note that the party gives permission, is not informed, that party has the right to set conditions? I would like you now to please look at item C, that: "A definite advantage ..." [In English] "... may accrue to the military efforts or economy of the enemy through the substitution of the above-mentioned consignments for goods which would otherwise be provided or produced by the enemy through the release of such materials, services, and/or facilities, as would otherwise be required for the production of such goods." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the party which provides permission for the passage of a convoy is authorised to assure that the other side does not draw any kind of military benefit from that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The UN was aware of this provision, and the UN -- my commander took particular care to make sure that -- within his powers, that the aid that was coming in was going to civilians. And in those cases, we would talk to the corps commander about the freedom of movement, understanding this document and this Article 23.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since this is not going to be admitted because the Geneva Conventions are part of the jurisprudence, can we now look at 1D1724, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting: General, sir, my learned friend Mr. Tieger very skillfully and successfully created the impression that Mladic forbade something -- or, rather, how Mladic confirmed that the freedom of movement was suspended, and then we did look at this document. This is P1786, but let's look at this document first. Allow me to read it, because I'm not sure if we have a translation of it. This is a regular combat report with the status at 1700 hours on the 12th of May, 1994. This is the Sarajevo Romanija Corps reporting to the Main Staff. And then down there in the last paragraph, it says: "At the check-point in Kasindolska Street, an armoured vehicle of the French Battalion was stopped, and during inspection it was established that the same is transporting seven boxes of mines for an 82-millimetre mortar, allegedly for their unit in Rajlovac." Can we now look at the next page, please: "An inspection established that these were not indicated as being among their arsenal of weapons of said calibre, and the resolution of this problem is underway. "In the area of responsibility of the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Battalion, we had the willful movement of true members of the UNPROFOR with an all-terrain vehicle in the direction of Kosevo, towards Visojevici, from where they were turned back." General, do you agree that transporting ammunition to the other side gives us the right to be cautious?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: First of all, I have no knowledge of this particular incident, and it was not my understanding and my duties, as military assistant to the sector commander, that we were aiding any particular side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can agree that there was no such assistance at higher levels, but this does not change the fact that at some lower levels, our enemies were supplied with weapons by passing through our lines, which did give us the right to be cautious and to step up inspections. Do you agree that if the other contracting party does not stick to the agreed rules and procedures, our party had the right to suspend a particular programme?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: You're asking me a hypothetical question and/or you're asking me to make a comment on a document which I haven't been able to verify the details of that statement, so I feel that I can't really answer that question professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, sir, this indicates something about an occurrence which you also spoke about, that there was a disruption or obstacles placed on the freedom of movement of convoys, and now I am speaking about the reasons for heightened control. This is not an attack on you or the UN, as a whole. All I would like to do is to throw some light on the reasons for heightened control on the part of the Serbian side and for need for more care.
