It's not that the Serbs were doing this because they were evil, but that they were taking measures in order to prevent themselves being used in the arming of their enemies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we deal with this, I would tell you again to refrain from making comments. The last point is just a statement on your part. Mr. Tieger, separate from the issue of translation, would you object to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's going to be MFI'd, in any event. I don't see anything at this point on which to object, but we'll have an opportunity to see if we can learn anything additional. But otherwise, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D769, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I feel the need to clarify why I made this comment. Well, it's not a comment. I would just like to inform the general that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, just ask questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in your statement of the -- actually, while we're looking for it: Are you aware that the Muslims or the Muslim Army used Unis's high-rise building, and the high-rise building of the Executive Assembly, and some other high buildings as sniper emplacements?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, we were aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend Mr. Tieger, on pages 23 to 25, asked you -- suggested that General Galic acknowledged that there were sniper actions throughout the town, but in the question it was acknowledged that General Galic admitted that there was sniper action against civilians. Did General Galic ever admit that there was sniper action against civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It seemed very clear, in the notes from that meeting, he was -- he was acknowledging that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are civilians mentioned anywhere?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Not specifically, but I did understand the sense of this statement from his own notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have notes from that meeting that would confirm that this referred to civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I do not have notes from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that different anti-sniper agreements were reached?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I do remember that we worked with both warring factions in Sarajevo for anti-sniper agreements. Our message to both warring factions was the same: to not engage civilians, and we would take actions against whatever warring faction did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, sir, that these anti-sniping agreements implied also a ban on sniper action in town against legitimate targets, not only against civilians; that this was a ban on sniper action in general?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I need to refer back to the agreements, but my understanding was that military actions against the other warring faction's military was the purview of the two warring factions. Where the UN engaged was when those military actions spilled over into the civilian community.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I now have P1208, please - this is a Prosecution document, P1208 - so that we can be reminded how, before this anti-sniping agreement was signed, one commander issued orders. One of these is unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please draw your attention to paragraph 3. Would you agree that here targets for snipers are being indicated quite precisely as being officers and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, those instructions are clear, not to engage civilians, children, on roads or buses. Yes, that's very clear there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This has already been admitted. We don't need to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall having information about how the French had video footage showing Muslim snipers firing at their own people and how they were preparing this? Actually, the French had this footage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I had heard those stories, but I had never seen the footage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 65 ter 09664.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you may not have seen the footage, but you did hear that such footage exists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I had heard the stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you also heard from the French that the Muslims filmed such attacks on children in order to broadcast it on TV and thereby blemish the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I heard those stories, and -- yeah, I heard those stories too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now look at this text, and let's try to identify it. This is an anti-sniping summary of FrenchBat 2, 23rd September 1994. This is the period while you were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the next page. We do not need the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at item H, which says "Location," and then point 7, which reads as follows: [In English] "According to a Bosniak --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bottom of the page. Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: She confirmed -- this Muslim woman confirmed to the French that the fire had come from the Bosnian Muslim side, opposite the PTT building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Well, that's what this sentence says on this document. What -- I'm just trying to figure out: What is this document? The previous one was a Frebat 2 document. Is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we show the witness the first page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an official report compiled by Captain Chassang. I apologise for my non-existent knowledge of French. It relates to an investigation of sniping incidents that was carried out by French Battalion 2, and the investigation concluded that the shots came from the Muslim-held building opposite the PTT. So as I say, this is an official report, provided by the French Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we not have the original French version in our e-court? It has the certain ERN number. I wonder whether we can show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could see the second page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour, I'm okay with this document. It's not normal that I would read this level of documentation, which is below -- it took me a while to catch up to where I was back then. Yes, I acknowledge the observations of -- in paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I surely accept that you haven't read it, but we are just talking about a phenomenon. That was the reason I asked you the question. Can we please tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D770, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, from whom did you hear about the filming of sniping attacks on the children in order to tarnish the reputation of the Serbs? Were these just rumours or were you informed of that, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It would have come from the UN -- our UN soldiers, and I seem to recall that a protest was lodged against the Muslims for these types of actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Had you ever heard or had you ever received any information to the effect that the Serbs would shoot at their own civilians in order to lay blame on the other side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I did not ever recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During our interview, you said that you had information about the Muslims' desire to provoke a foreign military intervention, but that you were not sure whether this sniping of their own people served that purpose. However, you did say that they had professional marksmen and snipers and that there were not at all any renegade elements. The sniping targeting their own civilians was a sort of military policy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I just want to answer all of the points of your question. Our assessment was that the Muslim authorities were interested in keeping the UN engaged with the operations, and, by extension, the international community. Secondly, I don't -- I don't recall ever saying that there was a military policy targeting their own civilians. I did say that the Muslims were guilty of targeting civilians, and we protested against them as we did protest against Serbs who fired against civilians. And the Muslims had their own professional marksmen and snipers, as did the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During our conversation, you also confirmed that UN officers had conducted investigations of the incidents in which members of the UN were the targets, and that in such instances, evidence was collected and a full investigation was carried out. On the other hand, when this involved civilians as being the target of fire, the UN conducted certain investigations with respect to the origin of fire but that the evidence was collected by the local police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That's correct, and we tried to get information from whichever faction was conducting their own investigation so we could complete our reports. And we were, to a greater or lesser degree, successful in getting the information to complete a thorough report, depending on what warring factions or parties were prepared to share with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But we both agree that in the criminal and legal sense, the targeting of civilians in Sarajevo was investigated by the local police?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: What I said was that where civilians were engaged, the UN would conduct its investigation, local authorities did what they did under their own national direction, and we tried to obtain information to complete our investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you conduct criminal investigations? Who collected the evidence? And I'm talking in the legal sense of the word. Was that the local police or was it the UN?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We did not conduct criminal investigations. We conducted simply an investigation to ascertain the facts and to determine which side was responsible for those incidents. In the event that any criminal activity was -- had occurred, we would bring in our own military police to conduct criminal investigations, but that was mainly pertaining to internal matters. When it came -- pertaining to sniping or shelling, that was just done by the UN troops on the ground, and the investigations were sent up the chain of command with their results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina shelled Sarajevo down-town?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In one case, we were aware of that. We conducted a joint investigation with the Muslim authorities. This was as a result, initially, by an attack that came from the Serb side. But in the course of our investigations, a second incident on the same position concluded that the second mortar attack came from the Muslim side. That information was provided back to the Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to your conclusions, what was the purpose of that second shell that was fired from a Muslim position? More precisely, was that an attempt to increase the number of casualties in order to accuse the Serbian side even more seriously?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The conclusions of our report was: First, that it was an attack from the Serbian side, which we protested back to the Serbs for attacking a civilian position. The second was that it was an attack on a civilian [Realtime transcript read in error "Serb"] position by Muslims, which we protested back to them. And we provided information to both warring parties and had a press conference about it to explain to them how we conducted the investigation, using the information back from the Muslim side, and we just presented our facts, indicating that both parties were at fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was whether you were able to answer -- gather the purpose on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would appear that the intent of the Muslims was to incite more casualties and put blame on to the Serbs for this attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember in which particular part of the town that happened?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: You are now taxing my memory on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when it happened?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I would have to go back through my notes, but I seem to recall it happened probably just west of Skenderija, in that area there on the Muslim side, near the market. But I'm really taxing my memory right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I have to remind you that in our earlier interview you mentioned your notes. Is there any way in which we can have access to these notes?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In 1997, when I provided my comment -- my report, whatever I had then was given, and I'm on record now as what I've said then, and I -- you know, all my subsequent comments have been based on that statement, and I have no idea where whatever information I had they used for that statement is today. So whatever documentation I had then is not -- I don't know where those notes are, other than what has been entered into evidence of my notes that I wrote up and the UN documents which I've seen referred to frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hand these notes over to the OTP personally?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Again, I just recall that whatever I had in 1997 was shared, it was the subject of how my report was produced, and I can't remember what happened to whatever I had back then. I don't have it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend Mr. Tieger advised us that they failed to locate it, which does not mean that we should refrain from trying to have them located and made available. And if the Trial Chamber could be of assistance, that would be very useful. You mentioned that Ganic was confronted with a number of your findings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I don't think the witness can see -- can scroll back the transcript. But for the purpose of the record, it's page 56, lines from 8 -- that should be a typo. If I can read it to you, could you confirm that it's a typo: "The conclusions of our report was: First, that it was an attack from the Serbian side ..." We are referring to the second attack from the Bosnian side. And then the transcript reads, I quote: "The second was it was an attack on Serb positions by Muslims, which we protested back to them." I take it "the Serb positions" should read "civilian positions."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that the Trial Chamber has taken note of our appeal for the notes to be found and made available, and that we shall have their support in our efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Robinson is certainly aware, and I believe the accused should be aware, that we were apprised of this situation before. Because of the potential ambiguity associated with that, we looked for the notes based on the representations made by Mr. Robinson. We have no indication that the notes were ever taken by the OTP and certainly no indication that we have those notes, despite an exhaustive search based on what we understood to be the premise that we had, in fact, been given the notes. As I understand it now, that's not the case. It's just no one knows what happened to them. But we would, in the normal course of business, of course, have recorded the receipt of those things, and there's no such indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just elaborate on that for a minute, not take very much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this something we need spend some time on that? We heard what the general said about this. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's okay, we can deal with it in some other form. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at least on one occasion, Ejub Ganic was speechless when you confronted him with the account of the conduct of the Muslim side towards their own citizens?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: He was speechless and not very happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that General Rose was convinced that Ganic had his own sniper detachment which was used for killing their own people around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that, according to the Geneva Conventions, and in this portion that we read today, number 4, Part 2, inter alia, hospitals should not be converted into military facilities and that they can only enjoy protection provided they're not used for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That's in accordance with the Geneva Convention, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Muslims open fire, from the Kosevo Hospital compound, on the Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then please have your statement, 11079, from 1997, and we need page 0055-5101. I think it's page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to the last paragraph, which reads: [In English] "Mortars fired from Kosevo Hospital and from the WCP Ilidza." [Interpretation] Does this refresh your memory about the abuse of the Kosevo Hospital and that this happened more than once?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I'll stand by my statement that I made in 1997. As I say, time has dulled my details. I do remember the missiles hitting the Presidency, and that I stand by the mortars were fired from the Kosevo Hospital and from the weapon collection point at Ilidza. But to your question about was this multiple times, I can only go by what my statement says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the Muslim side frequently used this tactic of shooting from the vicinity of UN installations, PTT buildings, and other facilities in order to attract a response from the Serbian side, and that because of that, the UN often lodged protests to Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is correct that the Muslims did this, and we did lodge protests back to the corps. I'm not saying just to Izetbegovic, but we did protest against the Muslim corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Do we still have time before the break, Your Excellency, for a new subject?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then that being the case, we'll take the break now for half an hour, and we will resume at five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly, I just wanted to take this opportunity to confirm our understanding that videolinks have been set up and scheduled for the 1st and 2nd of November for Witnesses KDZ476, 244, and 130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whatever the court schedule might be, we'll stick to those dates for those three videolink witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was my understanding as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your notice. Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I would like to remind you of your kind answers during our videolink meeting, when you confirmed that a siege can be a legitimate military tactic as long as it is not calculated to starve the civilian population. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is a tactic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, we agreed that it was a legitimate Serbian military target to encircle Sarajevo with the objective of keeping the Muslim Army in town and preventing it being used in fighting throughout Bosnia, thus confining the Muslim forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I would agree that it's legitimate for the Serbian military to encircle the Muslim forces inside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We also agreed that it was legitimate to use heavy artillery in order to: [In English] "... repel attack by the other side." [Interpretation] Use of heavy artillery in order to attack -- repel the attack by the other side, and that the Muslim side was superior in numbers, and that is why heavy weaponry was the Serbian element of some kind of strategic balance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I would agree that the use of artillery against Muslim forces, military forces, would be an appropriate strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agreed that the Muslim Army used mobile mortars to fire at Serbian positions, and that from time to time these mobile mortars were positioned near sensitive spots, such as UN headquarters and civilian zones, and so on and so forth, in order to draw a fire response from the Serbian side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Muslim forces did do that. We protested against them for using such tactics. And it was done in order to draw a response from the Serbs, but the Serbs had the choice of not to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to that. Whenever they could, they did not fire. We have documents about that. We also agreed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's a typical type of your statement. You don't have to make such a statement. Just ask questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also, we agreed that soldiers, fighters -- actually, that it was legitimate always to attack enemy fighters, regardless of where they happened to be, even when they are organising a football match near the front-line; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Engaging soldiers on either side was a legitimate activity, even if those soldiers were conducting sports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you remember, we agreed that all military headquarters, offices at all levels from company up to the corps, were legitimate targets, even when they were located further away from the line of separation or the front-line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I believe I've made this objection before. Maybe this is a good context in which to raise it. The question of military targets versus legitimate military targeting under circumstances are two different things, and the witness should be -- if it's a question of whether a particular military facility is legitimately targeted, then the witness has to be advised of the circumstances; place, location, type of weaponry, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm confident the general would be able to deal with this question. Could you answer the question, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Military headquarters are legitimate military targets by themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just for the purposes of information, this is the basis for specific questions that I mean to put on the basis of our interview. Also, depots are places where military supplies are obtained, where equipment is held, are also legitimate targets even if they are located in the depth of territory behind the front-lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Military depots and military supplies are legitimate targets. Where they are located provides a complicating factor, what you do with that military target. Now we're getting into an area of discernment for commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We also agreed that means of communication, vehicles, military transporters, transporters for equipment, public routes, factories for the production of military resources, are all also legitimate targets; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Military transports, transports for military equipment, factories producing military resources, are targets. Public routes, communications, vehicles that are not specified to be military, are not. It would have to be assigned to be military in purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean public routes. I meant military routes. Probably something was wrongly interpreted. Military routes. But we agreed that civilian commands, commands from where -- civilian commands or civilian heads of the military, such as the Presidency and similar bodies, can also constitute legitimate military targets, is that right, meaning locations of the civilian command and locations of the civilian heads of the military?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: To identify a military route would take an awful lot of explanations, so I would -- I'm not sure I've ever seen a purely military route in my life. Civilian commands or civilian heads of the military provides a somewhat nebulous area of -- for targeting, and that would require an awful lot of engagement with my -- with applicable legal staff to define if that was a legitimate target. I think that's the best way I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would now like to touch upon a set of questions relating to the proportionality and discriminatory fire, in view of your experience as a UN staff member, relating to the fighting in Sarajevo. Sometimes indiscriminate and disproportionate fire and shelling is talked about. I would like to be more precise about this. Did you know precise positions of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the town, itself? Did you know where these positions were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I knew where the Presidency was, the corps headquarters, and generally where the two confrontation lines were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know the disposition of the units that were both along the front or in the depth of the territory in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I did not have detailed information of every unit. That would have been known by the UN forces in the applicable areas. I dealt with the corps on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the Sarajevo area was covered by the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that that's where the 1st Corps was deployed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It was in the Sarajevo area, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the size or the strength of that corps?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We had assessments of size/strength of that corps within our own organisation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 1D406, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting: Did UNPROFOR have its own intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We had our own information services. Because we were the UN, we did not conduct intelligence; we conducted information-gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that for purposes of assessing who was firing from where, it would be necessary to know who was deployed where, which forces were occupying which locations?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That was important, and, therefore, we would always ask our own UN forces in the area to conduct the investigation and determine, based on their knowledge of the warring factions, what happened on the ground and who was where.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your amalgamated statement, on page 51, you say, and I can quote:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Q. Very well, Colonel. You said earlier -- or not earlier, but, rather, yesterday, asked by the Prosecution, your answer that, in fact, in Sarajevo there were only civilians and there were no military. Do you remember that? "A. When I said -- what I said was in specific areas, yes, there are civilians and the UN. There were -- the BH Army were along the confrontation line. They had their own headquarters, but there were other military targets. I mean, it is a big city. You have to be a little more specific." [Interpretation] Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I'll take it for granted that that's what I said because it's on my statement. I can't say I remember saying those exact words, but that's my statement. I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you locate the part of that statement? You said page 51, but I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down. I mean, if this is page 51, then -- can we look at the page before that. Yes, just one moment. We will look for the place. Perhaps the page is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting: General, sir, would you agree that an army - I'm sorry, this is on page 75, page 75 - that an army is obliged to place insignia on their soldiers and in that way make them look different from civilians? Do you agree that it is the obligation of each army to distinguish its soldiers and to place insignia and markings on the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It's a normal convention for armies to wear uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that, according to information and statements and information from Muslim generals, that in the beginning as many as 85 per cent of fighters fought while wearing civilian clothing? Later, this percentage was much smaller, but, nevertheless, completely identical to civilians.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I can tell you, as a professional soldier, that if an army has 85 per cent of its fighters wearing civilian clothing, that any engagement of those apparently civilians would necessitate a decision whether or not to shoot or not shoot based on the fact are they carrying a weapon, are they a threat to you? And I will tell you, from my experiences since then, our soldiers are taught that in the event that you're faced with potential combatants who are wearing civilian clothing, you would defer from shooting if they don't provide a threat to you. That is just one of the -- the fog of war that soldiers have to deal with every day, especially if you have 85 per cent of your fighters not -- wearing civilian clothing. That would just make it harder for commanders to engage them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let's finish with this statement. Do you see this part where it says: "Very well, Colonel," that part? Would you agree that that is a part of your statement where you talk about how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's wait. At page 75? Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question, General, would be: Would you agree -- since you're expecting a more specific question here, do you agree that there was no neighbourhood in Sarajevo that was purely a civilian one, one where there were no soldiers, no military elements, military installations, military buildings? Would you agree that each neighbourhood, all over town, there were military facilities?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I would not agree that each neighbourhood had military facilities in it. The city had an awful lot of civilians, and there were military units scattered throughout. But the inference that it was all military, no, I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you state -- I mean, if necessary, we can show you a map, but perhaps you can say on the basis of your recollection, what part of Sarajevo is it that was purely civilian and where there were no military installations at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Well, Sarajevo is a big city, so I could not properly answer your question which part of the city was purely civilian. My knowledge of Sarajevo was somewhat limited by my engagements with the corps and whatnot, so I could give you a general interpretation. I could show you briefly -- I have seen where the confrontation lines were, but I don't think I could properly answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that you understand that I have to be specific about any kind of general statement, because in the legal criminal sense, they cannot remain non-specific. Can we scroll this page down so that we can look at another question and answer related to this particular topic. "Very well. Colonel ..." Could you please look at this question and this answer. Does it not state here that you did not know about the disposition of these units and that you only dealt with the corps headquarters and with government agencies?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I did not know where the brigades were. That was the responsibility of the other UN battalions in the area. I limited my exposure to the corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you, nevertheless, agree that it is quite legitimate for the Serbian Army to fire on legitimate military targets within the city, itself?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I would agree that it's legitimate to fire against military targets, but with the Serb weapons systems they had, I would not have done it, as a Serbian commander, because I could not guarantee the effect of that weapons system against the target that it was going after.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 77 of this statement, please, two pages later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This answer that we can see here: "If there was a military target in the city, the Serbs had a right to go after the military target, and the UN would not protest that because that was within the rules of engagement." Do you agree, General, sir, that it was necessary to know completely the disposition or the distribution of the military targets within the town in order to be able to take a position? The United Nations should have taken a position in relation to any kind of firing event by the Serbian side, based on this answer that you gave here.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: And the UN position was, based on the detailed knowledge of the soldiers in the area, that if military targets were identified and engaged, we would not protest. But in those cases where they were not, we would protest. So I may not have the specific details. The question of specific military targets could be posed to those people who were in the areas that had that detailed knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's deal a little bit with the subject of proportionality and indiscriminate fire, or discriminate fire. In the Galic case, did you address the issue of proportionality and other related issues? In order to make it easier for you, let's look at page 81. Page 81: [In English] "Yes, I do understand." [Interpretation] Judge Orie: "Yes, I do understand." Could you please look at the question and the answer that you gave. Have you read this? This was your view; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we were to suppose that a Serb Army position was attacked from mortars or other heavy weapon from a building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you like to see the rest of the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be helpful, sir. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if the Serb Army positions came under attack from a mortar or any other heavy weapon from a building in a built-up area, would you counter this fire by using a sniper or would you use something else?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: You would use the weapons system to deal with the weapon that got -- that fired at you. And if you didn't have a weapons system that could deal with it, you wouldn't fire back. And I will refer you back to the UN position on the Igman Mount, where, in fact, our weapons systems were incapable of engaging the Serbs who were firing at us; therefore, we did nothing in reply. So to answer your question: If you are mortared and you can't fire back to engage the mortar, probably the decision is you just don't fire back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if, for example, mortar is being fired from a truck and inflicts losses on us, is it legitimate to return fire by using mortar as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No. In the scenario that you've painted, because it's a mobile system, you probably don't have a weapons system to be able to go after that mortar because you don't know where it's firing from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, you would agree with me that we cannot see that it's coming from a mobile weapon; we only see that we are suffering losses. In this scenario, what should an army do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, the Serbs made the decision to surround Sarajevo. And if you're suffering losses and you don't know where the firing is coming from, your only remit is to fire against the known military positions that are on the confrontation line, but not into the city, where the fire might be coming from. It's a soldier's dilemma.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if we do know where the fire is coming from and we can see it, is it a legitimate move to neutralise it? How can we eliminate the threat from a massive attack by mortars or any other weapons inflicting losses on us? If they're firing from -- at us from Golo Brdo or from a Howitzer near a military hospital, why should we be firing at Igman, at other locations, if the threat is coming from the former locations that I mentioned? So we should try and pre-empt or eliminate the threat -- the possible threat of us being attacked by mortars or perhaps some heavier weapons.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: If the Howitzer is firing at you which is located -- and that Howitzer is near a military hospital, if you've got a weapons system to take out the Howitzer, but, quite frankly, because it's beside a military hospital, you don't fire. Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was responsible for it being close to the military hospital; on the part of the Serbs or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The Muslims were responsible for firing the weapon, and we would protest against the Muslims for firing weapons near places like hospitals or the use of mobile systems, because it was trying to solicit a response not against the target, itself, but the collateral damage, and that was unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see now how you explain this on a concrete example. Can we have page 52 of the amalgamated statement, please. This portion that refers to Lukavica, can you please look at it from the beginning 'til the end.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Okay, I've read that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that if, for example, fire was being opened at the Serbs from Debelo Brdo -- and you know that Debelo Brdo was under the control of the Muslim Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Parts of it were. There was a UN post there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you agree, then, that there were no civilians at Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: There was a confrontation line there, yes, we acknowledged that, where there were no civilians probably within 100, 200 metres of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If fire was opened at Debelo Brdo, for example, those who were counting the number of shells, would these shells fired at Debelo Brdo be taken into account with respect to the total number of shells falling on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not quite sure that -- how to -- we counted numbers. I'm not quite sure if we counted the numbers that were fired on the confrontation line on Debelo Brdo on whatever day you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You cited Debelo Brdo as an example of disproportionate fire. Can we now briefly have Exhibit P1782. It's been admitted today into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to comment upon Mr. Karadzic's last comment, being that you cited Debelo Brdo as an example of disproportionate fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will say that when the Muslims fired at Lukavica, we protested the Muslims firing because we knew they were trying to incite a response from the Serbs. That was the first point. The second point, that in the area around Debelo Brdo there were military positions there, but there were also civilians, and the artillery rounds were going into civilian areas, at which point we protested, again, against the Serbians for firing those weapons systems into civilian targets. And, again, it's just a function of what weapons system were they using, and their firing was significantly greater than just defending themselves, but it was making a point, and there was extensive firing throughout that day, as I recall, and not just limited to the confrontation lines but actually going into civilian areas, which we had an obligation to report and stop. And that's what we tried to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to your page 52, and kindly understand that I really cannot leave any statement of yours as general as it is. We have to be precise. Look at the last sentence in paragraph 1, which reads --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought we were returning to the amalgamated statement, and in that connection I have a clean copy -- hard copy that might be of benefit to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It would be maybe a good idea for the general to have it in front of him, just in case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can go back to the statement immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please find page 52, where you say that the Muslims had fired at the Serbs and the Serbs returned fire. According to your statement, let's see which targets the Serbs engaged in firing back. Here, it says that the Serbs were firing at the city. Let's see exactly where at the city. They returned fire at Debelo Brdo and the zone immediately next to the River Miljacka on the Muslim side. Can you see here that fire was opened at Debelo Brdo, and do you agree that there is not a single civilian facility at Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that's just been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At one point in time, the general answered that there was a confrontation line there, and as he said, We acknowledge that where there were no civilians probably within 120 metres of it. And later, General, you said that certain fire went beyond that. So this may be a good opportunity to clarify, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree that the engagement was started maybe at the Debelo Brdo confrontation line. We were very careful that day because we had our own UN post there, and one round that hit the UN post would have violated the agreement, and we would have protested and defended ourselves. In addition to that, the reports were that it extended past the confrontation line, it was going into the civilian communities, because the confrontation lines were within hundreds of metres of civilians. And, again, I would, you know, state for the record that firing artillery against confrontation lines in an urban environment is going to cause a violation somewhere. It's an area weapons system, it's not the best weapons system to use against combatants in that scenario of an urban environment. So hopefully that, you know, elaborates on my statement there and answers the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 15 in e-court, and could you also please look at it, the response which starts: "The Muslims had their positions just below --" [In English] "... called Debelo Brdo. The UN were right on the top of it and the Muslim trenches were just below it. And if I could also say, then, the Serbs were just to the south of a higher piece of ground that looked down onto Debelo Brdo."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you like now to see a map or a photograph of Debelo Brdo, which shows that there are no civilian objects or facilities within at least 200 or 300 metres? Or maybe we can rely on your memory; therefore, we shouldn't resort to using a map or a photograph.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I've acknowledged that there were no civilians within probably 100 or 200 metres of the Muslim confrontation line or between the Muslims and the Serbs that dominated the high ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have again Exhibit P1782. 1782. In English is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the last sentence of the first paragraph, which says that one Famos employee was killed, and two women and one civilian were wounded, and then the last sentence in paragraph 3, which says that one girl and one woman, civilian woman were wounded. You may have noticed that this is a report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, addressed to the Main Staff, and reported here is the type and number of casualties and damage sustained by the Serbian Army from the Muslim side. Can we now look at the next page. Item 3, "Situation in the territory." The next page, please. Can you scroll down a bit, where it says: "At the time during the shooting and injuring of a child, the UN members of Debelo Brdo took shelter, and immediately after they came out, preventing our units from firing back. The UN members on Debelo Brdo conducted improperly even before, showing sympathy for the Muslim side. In particular, they supported the Muslim side in constructing shelters and moving towards our positions. The UN monitors were transferred to the security organ at the Slavisa Vajner Cica Barracks ..." Can we now look at the beginning of item 3, which reads: "Problems with the UNPROFOR ..." I believe you can see this first sentence: "Problems with the UNPROFOR in the Ilidza Infantry Brigade arose around 2115, when the UNPROFOR fired at our position in the area of the Forestry School, following our shooting at the Hrasnica-Igman road." General, can you see that this is about our responses to the fire coming from the Muslims, but, admittedly, also from the UNPROFOR, and that we are being fired at when we engage legitimate targets, and there's a shelter provided for the Muslim forces at Debelo Brdo which prevented us from responding appropriately?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Let me answer your question. UNPROFOR fired at the Serbian position in response to Serbs firing at us. We did not engage -- start that engagement; the Serbs did. Serbs had the right to respond to Muslim firing at them with the appropriate weapons systems, taking into account collateral damage. We did not debate that, but when it entered into the civilian realm, we did have issues with that. At no time am I ever aware that the UN ever assisted either warring faction, and in Debelo Brdo, not the Muslims factions, helping them dig their trenches. We don't do that. That was between Muslims and Serbs, fighting themselves. The UN forces in Debelo Brdo did go into cover to defend themselves, and we were in contact with them all day. And if they thought their lives were in danger, they had the right of self-defence, to fire back. But we did not initiate that engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General Milosevic reports that the Ilidza Brigade fired at Hrasnica-Igman road. This is a supply route for the Muslim Army in Hrasnica and Sarajevo. Someone from the UN fired at the Forestry School as a result of the fire opened at Hrasnica-Igman road, and then the UN forces went to Debelo Brdo in order to provide protection for the Muslim unit, which prevented us from responding. Now, can we go back to page 52 to look at another location in the town where we returned fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, you made an unhelpful statement. Refrain from making a speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I can put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General Milosevic is informing his main commander that the brigade fired at the Hrasnica-Igman road, after which UNPROFOR became involved, or do you believe that General Milosevic's report was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: General Milosevic can have his opinion, but we had troops on the Igman road, they were fired at, and they replied in defence of their own position. We were not the combatants here, not part of the warring factions; we were the peacekeepers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at the second location in the city where we fired back. The first one was Debelo Brdo, and the other one was the River Miljacka on the Muslim side. Do you agree that the River Miljacka in this particular section was a separation line? Do you agree that there were Serb and Muslim trenches on both riverbanks, and do you agree that on the Muslim side of the river there was a proper military fortification?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I agree that the river was the separation between the Muslim and Serbian forces, and it was interspersed with civilians throughout the riverbanks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In this answer, General, you didn't mention the firing going beyond the confrontation line, to the effect of engaging civilian elements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, could you direct me which answer to the question or is there a document I should be looking at now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "It was just fired at the city. In fact, it was firing around Debelo Brdo and the area just around Miljacka River on the Muslim side. It was -- it was intense." Not referring to this civilian element. If you could clarify, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The firing around Debelo Brdo, for the most part, was against the factions, the warring -- the front-line. But when it went down into the Miljacka River, it was interspersed with civilians down there. There was no 100-, 200-metre separation between lines and civilians; they were interspersed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, do you agree that both riverbanks, one or two metres from the river, there were trenches there, and that the neighbouring buildings were also used to defend this line? This was confirmed here by Mr. Sabljica as well. So we have trenches on both riverbanks, whereas on the other side there were fortifications occupied by the defender of the line?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I don't debate that there were defenders on both sides of the river and in buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D1758, please. 1D1758.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also a report by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command to the Main Staff of the VRS. Could we scroll up a little bit. If we don't have the translation, I would like to read the third paragraph, if I may. It's right there: "Engineering works are continuing in the area of responsibility of the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade, in the sector of the 2nd Infantry Battalion near Kudrine Kuce, and across from the Elektroprivreda, along the River Miljacka, where the entrenchment was carried out in the presence of UNPROFOR and in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade. At Elevation 850, it was noted that trenches were being dug. The digging was being carried out together by the soldiers of UNPROFOR and the Muslim soldiers, so we could see that along the Miljacka River, near Kudrine Kuce, across the road from Elektroprivreda, the fortification of lines was being carried out, although the shells were falling -- and if shells were falling along that particular sector of the Miljacka River, would that be legitimate?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: If the question is -- well, first of all, UN assisting Muslims with defensive works; no, we didn't do that. To have shells fired along the river, is that legitimate? In my understanding, no, because the proximity of civilians, buildings, the weapons systems, themselves, it just -- firing artillery in that proximity of the line is not an effective system. It is just too imperfect. You can't get the trajectories coming down onto the target; no. Use machine-guns, use rocket-launchers, use direct-fire weapons where you can put the weapon onto the enemy position, but indirect fire down there is not a good, legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just want to establish whether the Miljacka River was fortified at Kudrine Kuce and that that location was a section of that line. Also, General, sir, who is responsible for placing installations in a civilian zone? Is that our responsibility or theirs? Are they permitted to use civilian neighbourhoods as protection from retaliatory fire? Would that constitute a violation of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Using civilians at shields is illegitimate. Either party doing defensive works along there, it's well within their prerogative to do so. But that said, they cannot use civilians as part of their defensive works, and they have an obligation to get the civilians out of the area to allow the combat to go on with legitimate combatant parties. To allow the civilians to stay there is an abrogation of the responsibility of the respective commanders, and they will be held accountable in accordance with the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- can I remind you that at one point in time, you wanted to show the general 1D406, which is referring to a list of units, but you skipped it to show the general his statement. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will come to that document, certainly. It shows the forces of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army in town and around town. But I would like to tender the document that we were just looking at on the screen, please. And if there is no translation, then could it be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification, pending translation, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D771.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you agree that Muslim forces, by firing at Lukavica, also fired at an area where there were houses, a residential area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Firing at Lukavica, at the corps headquarters, would be a legitimate target; firing at residential areas would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lukavica was a residential zone; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: But it was also the corps headquarters, and we have to delineate, what were they shooting at?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there a difference, then, between Sarajevo and Lukavica, or there is some advantage being given to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Any engagement of Sarajevo/Lukavica would have been investigated to make sure that the targets being engaged were military targets, and I do not see any advantage being given to the Muslims. Both factions were treated fairly by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at page 60 of your statement, please, and I would like to have your answer, if there is any, about whether there is any difference between Lukavica and Sarajevo, in the sense that we were speaking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what's the point of this? You are admitting that Serbs violated Geneva Conventions by locating its headquarters in the residential area? Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, all I want to do is to see how the sides are being treated in the conflict by the international community or representatives of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you see this answer of yours here -- question and your answer: [In English] "Let's move on to talk about the specific example, Lukavica Barracks. Did you know that Lukavica was a residential area in Sarajevo?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Yes, I did." [Interpretation] You considered that firing at Lukavica was a legitimate action; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I said firing at Lukavica Barracks was a legitimate action. Firing at Lukavica, a residential site, would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And regardless of the fact that it was surrounded by a residential area, you, nevertheless, considered it legitimate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The barracks is legitimate, but we did protest against the Muslims for firing at the corps headquarters because of the reaction that that would have instilled. I've said that to you before. And if it hit the barracks -- if it hit the city, where the civilians were, the UN was consistent in its protest to whichever warring faction, and the Muslims would have been protested against firing against Serbian civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 58 of this statement, please. It's at the bottom of the page, where we have a question. There is your: "Okay. Let me just rephrase ..." And then there is a question by Judge Harhoff, and then your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at it. That was your answer at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I stand by the statement that firing at Lukavica Barracks was a legitimate target, and there was no indication from our troops on the ground that anything else but a military target was being engaged at that moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, would you not then have to know the complete disposition of Muslim forces in the Muslim area of Sarajevo, in the civilian zones, in order to be able to characterise Serbian fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The UN battalions and forces that were in Sarajevo were tasked to understand where the Muslim forces were so that when reports came back to us, we could properly report them and also, where necessary, apply the right protest. This was just a normal part of the UN reporting was to determine -- making sure that actions between warring factions was allowed to go on within those confines. But when outside that envelope, we had to intercede.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it is your position that striking at military installations or troops that happened to be in a civilian zone does not change the nature of that military target; is that correct? For example, that's how it was in Lukavica. Would that same thing apply to the Muslim installations in the town?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Striking military installations or troops is legitimate. Troops that happen to go in -- in accordance with your question, that happen to be in a civilian zone does change the nature of the target; that we will then start to decide whether you can engage the military aspect. If -- if you are in a civilian zone, you would probably stop it because of danger to the civilians. The report back for Lukavica -- Lukavica Barracks was that the French soldiers on the site said the rounds were hitting the headquarters. And while that is a problem for our own UN troops, because they were co-located, the fact that the headquarters was being engaged, well, that's just part of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, perhaps I put a confusing question. The question is this: The headquarters is in Lukavica, in a residential zone, just like all the Muslim military installations are located in Sarajevo in residential zones. Striking Lukavica in a residential zone, precisely or imprecisely, is legitimate. Is striking at Muslim military installations something that would have the corresponding status or is there any difference there? Yes or no. Would Serbian military installations located in a residential zone have the same status as Muslim military installations in residential zones?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Serbian military installations located in a residential zone have the same status of Muslim military installations in a residential zone. I agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D406, which I asked for earlier. I hope that there could also be a translation there. This is a document by the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its General Staff, and the document talks about the forces in Sarajevo. If there is no translation, let's just identify the document. The Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Army General Staff, Headquarters of the Army Administration for Organisational and Mobilisation. And it states at the bottom: "We are attaching an overview of new establishment titles and numbers of the VJ. "The information is to be used for internal purposes only, and it should not be copied." Could we look at the next page, please. And we have the 1st Corps here. First we have the General Staff of the Army, and then the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is located in Sarajevo, in the center of the city; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: If you're asking me the question, I can't tell from this document. If it says it's the organisation of the Muslim forces, I'll take it for -- for what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in your experience, do you recall that the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Supreme Command Staff were located in the very center of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree that the 1st Corps Command and the staff units were also located in the center of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please now direct you to 5667 on this page. That relates to the 1st Corps. Could you please look at that. And it states there: "BVP of the 1st Corps," and then: "5114: Battalion of DB, Battalion DB." Then the 1st LAR DPVO, then the 1st Engineers Battalion, and then the 1st LOB of the corps, then the 1st Medical Battalion. Can we look at the following page, please. And we can see here the 141st LBR, 104th, 145th, 146th, and then the Kralj Tvrtko Croatian Brigade in the town, itself, then the first map, the first MAD, then the Armoured Battalion of the 1st Corps, and then the NRC of the 1st Corps, then the Command of the Sarajevo Garrison, then the Command of Novo Sarajevo, then the Command of Vogosca, then the Command of Novi Grad, HQ of Ilidza, HQ of Stari Grad, HQ of Centar, and Command of Hadzici. Can we look at the following page. And then from 5454, we're looking at the 1st Corps again, 105th Motorised Brigade, 102nd Motorised Brigade, 105th Motorised Brigade, 111th probably Vitez Mountain Brigade, 112th Vitez Motorised Brigade, 115th Motorised Brigade, 152nd Motorised Brigade, 155th Motorised Brigade, Motorised Brigade, and 143rd Motorised Brigade. Would you agree, General, sir, that there were some 60 battalions in Sarajevo and about 150 companies? So we're having brigade battalions, or independent battalions, or companies and other units numbering around 150 companies and 60 battalions; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I acknowledge that there was a 1st Muslim Corps inside Sarajevo. I cannot attest to the number of companies or battalions, but I'm not debating there wasn't a corps in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see here, in the column "5063": "104th Vitez Motorised Brigade in Hrasnica"? Do you know the strength of the 104th Brigade in Hrasnica and its installations in Hrasnica, itself?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at 5453: "155th Motorised Brigade." Would you agree that the 155th Motorised Brigade was deployed in Dobrinja and that it had around 5.000 soldiers? And one witness said that he believed that they even had more. It's such a small area. You know the size of Dobrinja, don't you? Do you know where Dobrinja is?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I do. I can't attest that they had 5.000 soldiers, but I know the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the 155th Mountain Brigade's area of responsibility was in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I'll take your word for -- for that. I don't know the actual brigade, but there were troops throughout Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The new names are in the left-hand column, and the old names are in the right-hand column, for purposes of orientation. They were given new names, so this is what the change is. Can you see here that Pazaric is also under the responsibility of the 1st Corps? Do you recall that the 14th Division was there? The 12th was in the town, and in Tarcin and Pazaric, the 14th Division of the 1st Corps was located?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That's a level of detail I do not recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, for example, that if a brigade has from three to five battalions and a battalion has three to five companies, that that is a large number of command posts, substantial logistics of many forward command posts, and that the town of Sarajevo was chock full of installations that were required for this number of units?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That's a fair -- a fair comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you hear that Muslims were able to and did manufacture weapons, even new mortars as well as mortar shells, in the very center of Sarajevo, close to the television building?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I did know that there were factories in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I don't have any objection, Your Honour. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D772, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we have time. Do we have time for just one more brief document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D02498, please. 1D02498.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, I would just like to acquaint you with the document. This is a statement by Vahid Karavelic, whom you knew. Who was Vahid Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Karavelic, the 1st Muslim Corps commander, is that the same person we're talking about? I don't read -- I don't read these documents very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of the 1st Corps. I just wanted to look at one part of this statement of his so that we could see how he, as our direct opponent in war, views the artillery tactics of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. This is on page 13. I think it's perhaps on page 14. Maybe it's on page 13, because the first page is numbered as well. But there is a translation of this statement, there is a translation. While we're waiting for this -- there is a translation. I'm sure that there's a translation. I would like to read it, though. Can we look at the top of this document "Artillery Tactics," "Artillery Tactics of the SRK." Can we scroll this page down, please. Page 13, middle of page 13. No, no, the middle of the page, the subheading in the middle of the page. I'm going to read until we get the translation: "It seems that the SRK applied standard types of barrage fire; waves of fire, protective fire, selective fire, and concentrated fire. I did not notice a lessening of the artillery fire intensity during --" We have Mr. Tieger on his feet, so I'm going to wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We might be able to move quicker. It's 11377. We might find the English as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be the last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the English translation as well so everybody can follow more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So our direct enemy in war is providing the characteristics of the artillery fire of the Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We locate the relevant page, and the general can read it, and you can ask the question. Yes, that part. What is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would just like you to look at this passage. My question is: Do you agree that General Karavelic knew the disposition of his forces in Sarajevo very well and that this characterisation of his of the use of artillery by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is based on his knowledge of his own force's disposition, and that there is nothing illegal in this characterisation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: First of all, I know that General Karavelic knew the disposition of his forces, as the corps commander. The fact that he would have the understanding of Serbian doctrine for the use of artillery would be useful to him, but that being said, there is nothing that's legal for Serbian commanders to fire artillery into a city that is interspersed with civilians. It's the simple fact of the Geneva Convention and Rules of Engagement. It is not a black or white, it's legitimate or not; it has a number of different factors of military target, proportionality, collateral damage, and the fact that there were civilians inside the city would just negate the use of this type of weapons system.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I put just one more question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This paragraph speaks for itself, but I would like to ask you something else, General, sir. You said that you saw for yourself that people in Sarajevo suffered. Would this suffering have been less had the town been demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Could you just explain what you mean by "demilitarised"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Had there been a thorough demilitarisation and the town placed under the administration of the United Nations, so had there been a ban on fire and the existence of military forces in the town. This was something that was proposed by the Serbian side. Would the suffering have disappeared had there been a demilitarisation of the town, itself?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Well, first, to answer your question, the Serbians had a choice at the beginning not to fire into the town. That created the situation in the first place, by just containing the Muslim corps, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please, I would like you not to be answering some other question. Would demilitarisation have eliminated this suffering? As to whether we had a choice or not is something that we can discuss tomorrow. Would placing the town under the administration of the United Nations and demilitarising it have eliminated the suffering of the citizens? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It would have ameliorated the situation inside the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your indulgence. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Because of the time, I didn't want to intervene, but I think under normal circumstances, the witness should be permitted to answer the question and not be interrupted in mid-course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was advised, Mr. Karadzic, that you have had about two hours and fifty minutes, so you will have two hours and ten minutes to conclude your cross-examination tomorrow. Tomorrow, we are sitting in the afternoon, so we'll resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm hoping that I will get more time. I believe that I should be given more time, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You should be able to prioritise your questions and focus on relevant questions and be efficient. Probably you are well aware of this, General: During the course of your evidence, you are not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of October, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.
